segments.say: An issue is a brief with an address. That is the whole idea, and it is worth a sentence. Every brief we have written this week was typed into a terminal and lost when the session ended. An issue is the same words, kept, numbered, and readable by somebody who was not in the room. The words are the same words. What changes is where they live: off this machine, on a server, with a URL, visible to anybody with access to the repository, and still there when the laptop is shut. That is the whole difference, and it is the difference between a team and a person. There is also a version of this that is genuinely paperwork, and it is worth naming so you can avoid it. Filing an issue for something you are about to do in the next four minutes is theatre. Filing one for something a different session, or a different person, will pick up is the entire point. And there is a second thing an issue gives you that a terminal does not: a number. Something to close, something to reference in a commit, something to point at in three weeks and ask why that was not done. A conversation cannot be pointed at.

And read the instruction, because one clause in it is doing all the work. Read the review and the fix log. Pick the single most worthwhile thing still not done, small enough to fix in one change and real enough to matter. File it. Then stop. Do not fix anything. That last sentence is not politeness. An agent that finds a problem will fix it, because fixing is what it is for - and then the issue is a description of work already done and the whole exercise is theatre. Separating the finding from the fixing is what makes the issue an artefact somebody else could act on. The body shape is specified too: what is wrong, where, how to see it, and what done looks like. Four things asked for by name. There is a version of this instruction I would not write, which is find a bug and fix it. That produces work with no artefact anybody can review, and it produces it fast, which makes it worse rather than better.

And what it found is a good one. The alerts array in the feed grows without any limit, while the candle history sitting next to it is trimmed on every tick to a fixed window. One of those two was thought about and the other was not. That is exactly the kind of defect that survives a green suite and a careful review of each area separately, because neither half is wrong on its own - it is the inconsistency between them that is. And I want to be honest about how it found it, because it is not magic. It had a review document, a fix log, and the repository, and it was asked for the most worthwhile thing still undone. It did not go hunting through the code for novel bugs and it would not have been good at that. It read what was already written down about this project and picked the best item off it.

Which is a fair description of what a good engineer does on their second day somewhere. So read the body rather than the title. What is wrong, where, with the actual lines quoted. How to see it. And what done looks like. Three line numbers under Where: fourteen declares the array, thirty-seven pushes to it with no trim, and fifty-two scans all of it. A stranger could act on that, which is the only test an issue has to pass. Compare that with the brief we typed on the first morning. Same shape - what is wrong, where, what done looks like - and this one costs nothing to write because something else wrote it, and survives the session because it lives on a server. That is the entire upgrade.

And now the second agent gets the address, not the work. Read issue one. Create a branch named for it. Write a test that fails because of the bug and would pass once it is fixed - and run it, and watch it fail, before touching the code. Then fix it, run the suite again, commit with a message that explains the change rather than restating the diff, push the branch, and open a pull request that closes the issue. Notice how it starts: run gh issue view one and read it. I am not pasting the issue into the prompt. I am giving it the number and letting it fetch its own copy, which means the brief it works from is the one on the server, not a copy of a copy that has already drifted. Same clauses at the end as before: no questions, make the call, tell me what you chose. And run through what each of those steps is protecting. The branch protects main. The failing test protects against fixing the wrong thing, because a test that passes before the fix was never testing the bug. Running the suite after protects against fixing this and breaking that. The commit message protects the person reading the history. And the pull request protects against all of it being wrong in a way nobody looked at.

Notice that none of that is an agent instruction. That is how you would want a colleague to work, written down. The only reason it has to be written down is that this colleague has never worked anywhere, and has no idea that watching a test fail before you fix it is the difference between fixing the bug and fixing something adjacent to it. And watch the first thing it does. There was no branch naming convention in this repository, so it says so, picks one - issue, then the number, then a description - and tells me that is what it chose. That is the no-questions clause working as intended: a decision made and reported, rather than a prompt waiting for me. Then it does something I did not ask for. Before writing a test, it runs a throwaway node script against the simulator - a fixed seed, one instrument, eight hundred ticks - to watch the array grow. That is the step in between the issue and the fix, where you make sure the bug is actually the bug. There is also something worth noticing about what is not in the instruction. I did not tell it what the fix is. I did not tell it which files to touch. The issue says what is wrong and where, and everything else is its problem - which is only reasonable because there is a test suite, a branch and a review waiting at the far end.

And the last clause is the one I would keep in every version of this instruction: if the fix turns out to be bigger than the issue described, say so in the pull request rather than quietly widening it. Scope creep in a diff you did not write is the single hardest thing to spot in review, because everything in it looks reasonable and there is nothing to compare it against except an issue you read ten minutes ago. And the test on screen is the thing that makes any of that checkable. Seven hundred and fifty ticks, so the latest timestamp lands past the one-hour retention window, and then three assertions with the reason written into each one: the alert from tick zero must have been trimmed, leaving two; every alert still returned must be a recent one; and no retained alert may be more than an hour behind the latest tick. Those message strings are not decoration. When this fails in eleven months, the failure output is a sentence explaining what was supposed to be true, and that is the difference between a two-minute fix and an afternoon. The same clause has a second use, which is that it tells you when your issue was bad. If three pull requests in a row come back saying the change turned out to be bigger than described, the problem is not the agent - it is that your issues are describing symptoms rather than causes.

So it works, unsupervised, on a branch, with a test suite and a remote and a review step waiting at the end of it. And that combination is the point of the lecture. Nothing here trusts the agent. The branch means main is untouched. The test means the claim is checkable. The pull request means somebody looks. Take any one of those away and you are back to hoping. And the fix is seven lines. A trimAlerts function that walks forward from the front of the array while the timestamps are older than the cutoff, and one splice; then a single call added after the push, on the line right below it. That is what the issue asked for and nothing else. All twenty-nine tests pass, and it says out loud that this is a minimal scoped fix matching the issue exactly, no widening needed - which is it answering the clause I gave it rather than me having to check. One commit, pushed to the branch, and a pull request opened. Two hours of work in this course now exists as a numbered thing on a server that somebody else can disagree with. And while it works, this is the moment to say what this lecture replaced. The reference course installs a hosted agent that watches a repository and does this on a webhook. It is a good product. What it is, underneath, is the four commands you are watching, triggered by an event instead of by a person - and if you can drive them by hand you can decide for yourself whether you want them triggered automatically, on which repositories, with whose credentials.
